newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: War crimes suspect was on traffic duties - witness.
newsitem.headline: War crimes suspect was on traffic duties - witness.

text.p: A former police officer in authority over Bosnian Serb Dusko Tadic told the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia on Wednesday neither he nor his men took part in any illegal activity during the Bosnian war.
Tadic is accused of killing, raping and torturing non-Serbs as part of an "ethnic cleansing" campaign in the Prijedor area of northwest Bosnia in 1992. He denies the charges.

Duro Prpos, Tadic's shift commander in the Prijedor traffic police at the time he is accused of carrying out some of the atrocities, was testifying as a defence witness via live satellite link from the Bosnian city of Banja Luka.

"I wish to say here my conscience is quite clear. My responsibility was to control traffic and I and my policemen did not take part in anything beyond that," he said in response to questioning about his knowledge of war crimes in the area.
Prosecution witnesses have testified that Tadic took an active role in rounding up his Moslem neighbours for deportation to prison camps where he and other Serbs maltreated them.
Prpos said he had not been aware of any forced removal, or "ethnic cleansing", of Moslems in the Prijedor area during 1992.
"As far as I know, they were not forcibly removed but they went of their own free will," he said.
Pressed by the cross-examining prosecutor for clarification, Prpos said thousands of Moslems had left Prijedor voluntarily.
"Conditions were such that whoever could leave did leave. They knew what would happen during the war and they went voluntarily," he said.

Prpos's testimony has focused on police records which the defence says show Tadic to have been working at a checkpoint during the time some of the alleged atrocities were committed at camps several kilometres (miles) away.

He said he inspected the four checkpoints under his authority at random times of the day and night, and sometimes several times a day, so the officers on duty would not have been forewarned of his arrival.
At no time had he ever found any man absent from his post, he said.
Tadic's lawyers asked for defence witnesses to be allowed to testify from Bosnia, saying some were unwilling or afraid to travel to The Hague for fear they might be arrested.
The judges ruled in June that, because of the difficulties of conducting a trial relating to a recently ended conflict, it was "in the interests of justice" to allow remote testimony.
They stressed this was an exception to the general rule that witnesses must testify in The Hague, adding that testimony via satellite would not weigh as heavily as evidence given in court.
The Tadic trial is expected to finish in November and the judges are expected to deliver their verdict in the spring.
So far the Hague tribunal, set up by the U.N. in 1993, has indicted 75 suspects from the various ethnic communities in the former Yugoslavia.

More than 50 of them are Serbs, including the former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic who are charged with genocide for slaughter of up to 6,000 Moslem civilians in Srebrenica.
The tribunal holds seven suspects in its Hague cells, the rest remain at liberty.
